account: South Wales Police and Gwent Police are the first UK forces with the Operator Initiated Facial Recognition (OIFR) app. It lets an officer photograph a person on a police phone and compare the image with a reference database. It is for when the person refuses or gives false details. In 2022 the National Physical Laboratory tested the NEC NeoFace V4 algorithm that the app uses, under contract to the Metropolitan Police and South Wales Police. The app launched in December 2024. In one use, an officer in Cardiff identified a 38-year-old man wanted on a European arrest warrant since 2012. The warrant was for drug dealing and assaulting a police officer with a weapon in Poland. He was remanded in custody to Westminster magistrates' court (Wales Online, 14 July 2025). The arrest date is not given. The forces report 50 South Wales searches producing 10 arrests, and six Gwent uses with three matches and one arrest. They cite the National Physical Laboratory testing, in which the correct match came top for people in the database (Wales Online). The accuracy claim rests on those 2022 tests. More than 500 officers had been trained by July 2025 (Emergency Services Times, 15 July 2025). In an audit report of August 2025, the Information Commissioner's Office said that it had observed the app at the two forces and called it a pilot in its infancy. In August 2026 the Information Commissioner's Office still described the app as a pilot in a limited number of forces. No source reports the outcome of the extradition proceedings.

ai_role.statement: The app compared a photograph taken on a police phone with a reference database and returned the match that identified the man. Officers then confirmed the warrant and detained him. In 2022 tests for the Metropolitan Police and South Wales Police, the National Physical Laboratory found that the NEC NeoFace V4 algorithm used for OIFR returned the correct match first for every probe image of a person in the database. NPL ran those tests offline, without officers taking the photographs or judging the matches. No source gives the match score in the Cardiff case.

fields.account: South Wales Police and Gwent Police are the first UK forces with the Operator Initiated Facial Recognition (OIFR) app. It lets an officer photograph a person on a police phone and compare the image with a reference database. It is for when the person refuses or gives false details. In 2022 the National Physical Laboratory tested the NEC NeoFace V4 algorithm that the app uses, under contract to the Metropolitan Police and South Wales Police. The app launched in December 2024. In one use, an officer in Cardiff identified a 38-year-old man wanted on a European arrest warrant since 2012. The warrant was for drug dealing and assaulting a police officer with a weapon in Poland. He was remanded in custody to Westminster magistrates' court (Wales Online, 14 July 2025). The arrest date is not given. The forces report 50 South Wales searches producing 10 arrests, and six Gwent uses with three matches and one arrest. They cite the National Physical Laboratory testing, in which the correct match came top for people in the database (Wales Online). The accuracy claim rests on those 2022 tests. More than 500 officers had been trained by July 2025 (Emergency Services Times, 15 July 2025). In an audit report of August 2025, the Information Commissioner's Office said that it had observed the app at the two forces and called it a pilot in its infancy. In August 2026 the Information Commissioner's Office still described the app as a pilot in a limited number of forces. No source reports the outcome of the extradition proceedings.

purpose: Built to confirm the identity of a person an officer suspects is missing, at risk or wanted when they cannot or will not give details. This identification was that use.

ratings.reason: South Wales Police identified in Cardiff a man wanted on a 2012 European arrest warrant and remanded him. It reports 10 arrests from 50 app searches. A measurable result for the forces, on their own figures as relayed by the press.

One man wanted for drug dealing and assaulting an officer with a weapon in Poland was taken into custody for extradition proceedings. The reports give no further harm prevented. So the public benefit is the execution of a warrant.
